key_insight: Introduce "tensor similarity", a weight-space metric for tensor-based models that is invariant to weight-space symmetries, enabling verification that two network components implement the same computation even out-of-distribution.
problem_solved: Bridges the gap between empirical-behaviour similarity (which fails OOD) and naive parameter comparisons (which break under basis symmetries), providing a principled, symmetry-aware way to test mechanistic equivalence of network parts.
method: Define a tensor-aware similarity metric that compares multilinear operators (tensors) rather than raw parameters, factoring out basis and symmetry transformations.
Compute similarity by aligning or mapping tensor factors (e.g., via constrained optimization or tensor decompositions) to remove permutation/scale/orthogonal symmetries common in weight space.
Validate the metric on representative tensor-based modules, showing consistent identification of equivalent computations where empirical metrics fail.
impact: Gives interpretability researchers and model engineers a robust tool to confirm when components/circuits are truly the same across architectures or reparameterizations, improving model auditing, transfer of mechanistic findings, and reliable model editing.
visual_elements: Side-by-side diagram of two network modules with their tensor representations and an arrow labeled "tensor similarity" showing alignment/invariance.
Illustration of common weight-space symmetries (permutations, scalings, orthogonal transforms) with a visual showing the metric is unchanged.
Small bar/line chart comparing tensor similarity vs empirical-behaviour similarity across in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings.
Flowchart of practical uses: identify equivalent circuits → transfer interpretations → targeted editing/patching.
paper_title: When Are Two Networks the Same? Tensor Similarity for Mechanistic Interpretability
paper_authors: ML Nissen Gonzalez, Melwina Albuquerque, Laurence Wroe, Jacob Meyer Cohen, Logan Riggs Smith
